On modeled datacenter and edge NPUs, LWS hides Learning within Prediction, sustaining Prediction-only throughput while preserving 99.3% of fully fresh Learning's quality benefit for TTT-E2E 3B at 128K tokens. Across nine models, LWS achieves 1.6x the throughput of serial execution and 1.3x that of the best prior co-execution architecture. RTL synthesis shows that LWS adds 1.5% to NPU core area without another MAC array. By efficiently turning idle inference capacity into learning capacity, LWS establishes inference-time learning as a first-class workload for future LLM accelerators.

AI.title_translation: 可变推理：为推理时学习设计LLM加速器
AI.tldr: 本文提出了一种名为LWS的LLM加速器架构，通过在推理过程中利用空闲算力进行学习，实现了推理时学习，同时保持高吞吐量和学习质量，并显著优于现有架构。
AI.motivation: 长上下文LLM需要处理不断增长的历史信息，但全注意力机制导致每个新token的成本越来越高。推理时学习（ITL）提供了一种替代方法，即模型在推理期间继续在上下文上进行训练，并将学习到的内容保留在其权重中。然而，现有的推理加速器假设权重固定，而训练加速器则针对完整的训练步骤，无法高效地支持同时进行学习和预测。
AI.method: 本文提出了学习时服务（LWS）架构，这是一种推理加速器，它在对延迟敏感的预测和对截止日期灵活的学习之间共享计算硬件。LWS通过以下方式实现：1) 利用注意力机制的非矩阵操作产生的空闲矩阵容量进行学习；2) 允许部分层延迟权重更新，同时保持较小的质量损失；3) 硬件管理的逐层权重版本控制，允许学习发布更新，而正在进行的计算读取旧版本；4) 可恢复的规约块，允许学习内核跨越零碎的空闲窗口并让位于预测；5) 专用的softmax梯度单元缓解向量争用。
AI.result: 在建模的数据中心和边缘NPU上，LWS将学习隐藏在预测中，维持了纯预测的吞吐量，同时对于TTT-E2E 3B模型在128K tokens下保留了99.3%的完全新鲜学习的质量优势。在九个模型上，LWS实现了串行执行1.6倍的吞吐量，以及优于现有最佳协同执行架构1.3倍的吞吐量。RTL综合显示，LWS仅增加了NPU核心面积的1.5%，无需额外的MAC阵列。
AI.conclusion: LWS通过高效地将空闲推理能力转化为学习能力，将推理时学习确立为未来LLM加速器的一类重要工作负载。
AI.translation: 长上下文LLM必须保留不断增长的历史信息，但全注意力机制使得每个新token的成本越来越高。推理时学习（ITL）提供了一种替代方法。模型在推理期间继续在上下文上进行训练，并将其所学保留在权重中。最近的工作表明，ITL可以在仅关注最近固定大小窗口的情况下，达到与全上下文注意力机制相同的质量。这限制了注意力成本，但除了预测（前向传播）成本外，还增加了学习（反向计算和权重更新）成本。推理加速器假定权重固定，而训练加速器则针对完整的训练步骤。本研究发现了两个机会。注意力的非矩阵操作留下了足够的空闲矩阵容量用于学习，而选定的层可以容忍延迟的权重更新，且质量损失很小。我们通过“学习时服务”（LWS）利用了这两点，这是一种推理加速器架构，它在对延迟敏感的预测和对截止日期灵活的学习之间共享计算硬件。硬件管理的逐层权重版本控制允许学习发布更新，而正在进行的计算读取旧版本。可恢复的规约块允许学习内核跨越零碎的空闲窗口并让位于预测，而专用的softmax梯度单元缓解了向量争用。在建模的数据中心和边缘NPU上，LWS将学习隐藏在预测中，维持了纯预测的吞吐量，同时对于TTT-E2E 3B模型在128K tokens下保留了99.3%的完全新鲜学习的质量优势。在九个模型上，LWS实现了串行执行1.6倍的吞吐量，以及优于现有最佳协同执行架构1.3倍的吞吐量。RTL综合显示，LWS仅增加了NPU核心面积的1.5%，无需额外的MAC阵列。通过高效地将空闲推理能力转化为学习能力，LWS将推理时学习确立为未来LLM加速器的一类重要工作负载。
AI.summary: 本文提出了一种名为LWS（Learning While Serving）的LLM加速器架构，旨在支持推理时学习（ITL）。传统LLM在处理长上下文时面临注意力成本高昂的问题，而现有加速器不适合同时进行推理和学习。LWS通过共享计算硬件、硬件管理的权重版本控制、可恢复的规约块和专用softmax梯度单元，利用推理过程中产生的空闲计算资源进行学习，从而在不牺牲预测吞吐量的前提下，实现了高效的推理时学习。实验结果表明，LWS显著提高了吞吐量，并保持了高质量的学习效果，且硬件开销极小，为未来LLM加速器中的ITL提供了可行方案。
AI.keywords: 推理时学习, LLM加速器, LWS, 异构计算, 硬件架构
AI.comments: 这项工作极具创新性，它巧妙地解决了LLM长上下文推理中注意力成本高昂的问题，并首次将推理时学习（ITL）提升为LLM加速器的一等公民。其核心创新在于LWS架构能够智能地利用推理过程中的空闲计算能力进行学习，通过硬件级的资源共享和调度机制，实现了预测和学习的协同并行，而传统加速器通常将两者视为独立任务。特别是，逐层权重版本控制和可恢复规约块的设计，有效解决了延迟敏感的预测与灵活的学习之间的资源冲突。LWS在保持高吞吐量和学习质量的同时，仅增加极小的硬件面积，这显示了其巨大的实际应用潜力。这项研究为未来LLM加速器的设计开辟了新思路，有望显著提升LLM在动态和持续学习场景下的效率和适应性。

title: EventSpikeSeg: Memory-Aware Mixed-Signal Architecture for Event-Camera Spiking Segmentation
summary: Event-camera segmentation requires persistent neural state despite sparse input events, making memory organization a central constraint on embedded implementation. We present EventSpikeSeg, a mixed-signal architecture combining resident capacitor memory with shared analog processing in GF180MCU 180-nm CMOS. Its 25-population spiking encoder-decoder has 143,824 synaptic weights but requires 30,976,000 membrane states at 440 x 640 resolution. The mapping specifies chronological 5-ms model updates, digital event/address services and 64-state capacitor banks. Characterization covers 22 module families and 74 operating points, distinguishing transistor simulations from digital-library estimates. Nominal results include 41.711 microwatts biased neuron-core power, 3.338-pJ positive terminal energy for a 1.4-microsecond cell read, and 0.531-mV selected-state drift over a 5-ms extracted-tile hold. Commit and coupling errors are reported separately. The software checkpoint records 27.976% mean intersection-over-union on a held-out six-class DSEC split; this is not hardware accuracy. Component layouts and simulation evidence quantify local implementation costs and expose storage replication and service scheduling as scaling constraints. A detailed SPICE-calibrated behavioral forward simulation of one full-resolution DSEC frame achieves 24.26% mean intersection-over-union, versus 26.22% for the matched PyTorch reference, using a compact 5-fF bank variant and external count/voltage calibration. Physical full-network operation, system energy and mismatch robustness remain unverified.

title: WaferTetris: Efficient Freeform Mapping on Wafer-Scale Accelerators
summary:
Wafer-scale accelerators offer massive compute capacity through hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs) interconnected across a single wafer, but realizing this potential requires efficient application mapping. Their scale makes programming these systems and mapping applications onto them challenging. Existing approaches rely on template-based mappings to maintain productivity, but these templates restrict the mapping design space. In particular, they impose fixed geometric layouts over the PE grid, often leaving compute and memory resources underutilized.
  In this work, we present WaferTetris, a system that removes these geometric restrictions through freeform mapping. Its Tetris-like strategy flexibly packs computation across the wafer, improving PE utilization and usable memory capacity while preserving PE-task code. We develop a recurrence-based throughput model that captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism, and an architecture model with per-color gates that enable existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms to enforce WSE routing constraints.
  We evaluate WaferTetris on Cerebras WSE-3 using LLM decoding and scientific stencil benchmarks. For LLM decoding, it achieves up to $4.42\times$ the system throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline on the same fabric size. Compared with the manually optimized WaferLLM, WaferTetris supports $1.8\times$ the context length for LLaMA3.1-8B (80k versus 44k), while delivering equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths, up to $1.10\times$.

title: eDIAR: Training-Free Open-Speaker Streaming Diarization for Long Meetings and Large Archives via e-means
summary: Meetings last up to an hour, and nobody knows in advance how many people will speak. Neural diarizers with a fixed number of output slots, such as Streaming Sortformer and Nemotron-3, are accurate and run online, but they cannot name more speakers than they have slots. We remove this limit without retraining. The slot head keeps deciding who is active and when speech overlaps, and speaker embeddings are clustered inside a single slot, with the official e-means algorithm, only after every slot has been used. In the streaming system, re-clustering is confined to a bounded window, labels are revised for a few seconds, and identities are anchored to the slots of the head. The resulting system has no limit on the number of speakers and stays accurate when speakers outnumber the slots, where fixed-slot models break down. On meetings that grow to an hour it stays far more accurate than Streaming Sortformer, which accumulates errors, and its cost per update does not grow with the meeting. The same recipe turns the four-slot Streaming Sortformer into an open-speaker system. Across recordings, e-means makes it affordable to link the speakers of a large archive frame by frame, a task that arises when conversational corpora are prepared, and it reaches the clustering quality of Lloyd's $k$-means several times faster. The method needs little tuning, and e-means runs with its default recipe from a few hundred to more than a million embeddings.

title: Understanding Contextual Bias in Agricultural CNNs Through Hidden-Neuron Concept Induction
summary: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images using background-dominated patches that contain little or none of the target object, showing that they exploit contextual information. Previous studies detected this behavior through classification accuracy but say little about what CNN hidden layers represent. We investigate whether Concept Induction can reveal interpretable visual properties associated with hidden-neuron activations on contextual image patches. Using five agricultural datasets with high, moderate, and low contextual bias, we analyze four CNN architectures at three network depths and five patch locations. Quantitative image descriptors of each patch are encoded in a knowledge graph and used as background knowledge for Concept Induction, which derives logical expressions characterizing neuron activation. These expressions are tested on held-out images using the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta. Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated. Validation was most frequent at intermediate depths (mean 40.2% at mid layers versus 12.0% at deep layers), and no patch location dominated across datasets. Among the tested descriptors, edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features had the highest validation rates. Stronger contextual bias did not correspond to higher neuron-feature validation rates: moderately biased Sugarcane had the highest rate (40.5%) and highly biased Cassava the lowest (19.2%). These results suggest that behavioral context dependence and the semantic interpretability of hidden neurons capture different aspects of CNN behavior, and that Concept Induction can complement patch-based bias detection.

title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.

title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.

title: Impact of Grid-Forming Inverter Placement and Penetration on Local and Aggregate Frequency
summary: Modern power systems are undergoing a huge shift in generation mix, including inverter-based resources that are fundamentally changing the stability dynamics of the grid. Thus, synchronous Generators (SG) are gradually being displaced by Grid-forming inverters (GFM) that are proposed as a solution to continue supporting grid stability. However, the effect of GFM placement in the network on frequency performance and how well aggregate-frequency assessment captures placement sensitivity observed in local frequency metrics remains unclear. This paper evaluates all SG and droop-controlled GFM assignments in the IEEE 39-bus system. A reduced-order model is used for the exhaustive search with load disturbances applied separately at every eligible load bus while considering nadir and Rate of Change of Frequency (RoCoF) derived from both device rating weighted aggregate frequency and local bus frequencies. Results reveal that at fixed GFM penetration, placement produced up to 104 mHz variation in worst-case local nadir and 0.21 Hz/s in maximum local RoCoF. Aggregate-frequency assessment reduced the apparent across placements by 89\% for nadir and 88\% for RoCoF at 50\% GFM penetration. These results indicate that aggregate-frequency assessment alone may obscure favorable or adverse placement effects on local frequency performance.

title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
summary: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.

title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comments: 9 pages, 5 figures. Code, videos and results: https://zhanghutony.github.io/ibmarl/. A preliminary version appeared at the PhysCollaBot Workshop at IROS 2026
summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Code, videos and results: https://zhanghutony.github.io/ibmarl/. A preliminary version appeared at the PhysCollaBot Workshop at IROS 2026

title: Tight Bounds for k-Median++ and Improved Bounds for k-Means++
summary:
The popular $k$-means++ algorithm, or $D^\ell$-sampling, is a fundamental primitive in both the theory and practice of clustering. In the bi-criteria setting, the algorithm samples $k+Δ$ centers ($Δ\ge0$), and its cost is compared with the optimum using $k$ centers. Despite extensive study over the past two decades, its exact approximation ratio and tight bi-criteria guarantees remain unknown.
  We give a unified analysis for every distance exponent $\ell>0$, every $k\ge1$, and every $Δ\ge0$. For metric $k$-median, our bounds are tight for all $k$ and $Δ$. Without extra centers, the exact approximation ratio is $2(1+H_{k-1})$ (also in Euclidean space), improving the previous upper bound by a factor of $2$ ($H_j$ denotes the $j$th harmonic number). This tight analysis reveals that even one extra center improves the approximation ratio by an additive $Θ(\log\log k)$, whereas previous bounds show no improvement.
  For every $\ell>0$, our analysis gives upper bounds with the same dependence on $k$ and $Δ$ as our tight bound for metric $k$-median, with leading constants depending only on $\ell$ and whether the metric is Euclidean. Beyond the improved dependence on $Δ$, our leading constants are smaller than those in previous analyses. In particular, for the widely used Euclidean $k$-means objective, our upper bound without extra centers is $(1+\varphi)(1+H_{k-1})$, where $\varphi\approx1.618$ is the golden ratio, improving upon the previous constant of $5$. With oversampling, a constant fraction of extra centers is known to provide a constant-factor approximation. For example, with $10\%$ extra centers, our guarantee is $5.7$, compared with the best previous guarantee of $25.9$.

title: From smoothed analysis to backward error: The power of adaptive perturbations
summary:
Smoothed analysis has become a central tool in theoretical computer science, often allowing for significant improvements to worst-case running times if we settle for a solution to a small random perturbation of the problem instance. This is closely related to the classical concept of backward error in numerical analysis, which allows an algorithm to return a solution to an arbitrary perturbation of the problem.
  Despite the qualitative similarity of these concepts, we show that they can exhibit large quantitative differences. Notably, we prove that, while a linear system with any $n \times n$ matrix $A$ can be solved to backward error $ε$ using $O(\log(n) / ε)$ matrix-vector products with $A$, any algorithm that solves a random $ε$-sized perturbation of $A$ requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products. This means that a useful perturbation for solving a linear system in backward error must be adaptive to the input. Interestingly, however, randomness is still essential: we show that any deterministic method that attains small backward error for all linear systems provably requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products, resulting in the first separation between randomized and deterministic algorithms in a natural computational model for solving linear systems. Finally, we show that matrix structure can significantly affect backward error complexity. For example, we show a deterministic $O(1/ε)$ matrix-vector product algorithm for symmetric linear systems.

title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
comments: Accepted for publication in International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR). 21 pages, 18 figures
summary: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.
comment: Accepted for publication in International Journal of Robotics Research (IJRR). 21 pages, 18 figures

title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple
summary: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

title: Restoring Diversity in Distilled Image and Video Generators by Probing Activations
summary: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.

title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
comments: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Code and leaderboard available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench
summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Code and leaderboard available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench

title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://github.com/kyotovision-public/bal
summary: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://github.com/kyotovision-public/bal

title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
summary: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
comments: 10 pages, 5 figures, accepted at the 13th IEEE Special Session Privacy and Security of Big Data of IEEE BigData 2026
summary: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, accepted at the 13th IEEE Special Session Privacy and Security of Big Data of IEEE BigData 2026

title: The Cranston--Li--Su--Wang--Xu (2026) conjecture is true
summary: Let $A$ be a finite abelian group. A nowhere-zero $A$-flow of a graph can be changed along a cycle: going around the cycle, add a fixed non-zero element of $A$ to the value of every edge that points forward and subtract it from the value of every edge that points backward. The Cranston--Li--Su--Wang--Xu (2026) conjecture on the reconfiguration of nowhere-zero flows states that if $A$ has at least four elements, then in every graph in which all degrees are even, any two nowhere-zero $A$-flows are joined by a chain of such changes through nowhere-zero $A$-flows. It also states that, for every integer $k\ge 4$, the same holds for integer flows whose values are between $1$ and $k-1$ in absolute value, where each change adds a non-zero integer. We prove this conjecture. The proof is by induction on the number of edges. If a flow enters a vertex along one edge and leaves it along another edge with the same value, the two edges can be replaced by a single edge; this gives a smaller graph. The main step is to change every flow into a flow with such a pair of edges. For $A$-flows we do this when all degrees are at most $4$; repeatedly replacing a vertex of degree at least $6$ by a triangle, following Cranston et al., reduces the general case to this one. For integer flows, we show that, in a graph in which all degrees are even, any two nowhere-zero flows with values in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_k$, $k\ge 4$, are joined by changes that add only $1$, $-1$, $2$ or $-2$, and that such changes lift to integer flows. All theorems of this paper are also proved in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

title: Curvature-Aware Edge Dynamic GNNs for Low-$p_T$ Track Reconstruction at HL-LHC
summary: Particle track reconstruction in high-energy collider experiments is a computationally demanding combinatorial problem, traditionally solved by Kalman filters that scale poorly with increasing detector occupancy. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative. In this work, we introduce the Manifold Helical-IN, a novel Interaction Network architecture that explicitly embeds detector spacepoints onto a helical manifold chart using curvature-aware features. This geometric projection mathematically unrolls the tightly curling trajectories of low-momentum particles. Consequently, the network can distinguish true physical tracks from combinatorial noise with good precision. Evaluated on the TrackML challenge dataset, the proposed Manifold Helical-IN achieves a reconstruction efficiency of 0.9675 in the experimentally critical $p_T > 0.5$ GeV regime, approaching recently reported Transformer-based approaches. Crucially, the manifold embedding yields a fake track rate of 0.0037. This represents a 13-fold improvement over the baseline Helical-IN (0.0508). Furthermore, the model maintains good track coherence, as quantified by our proposed Mean Hit Recovery Fraction (MHRF) of 0.858, and achieves a highly efficient inference latency of approximately 150 ms per event on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. These results represent a critical step toward real-time soft particle tracking for the High-Level Trigger (HLT). By operating within practical HLT latency budgets, this geometry-aware approach provides a pathway to recover soft, anomalous Beyond Standard Model signatures such as unclustered energy patterns (SUEPs), that routinely evade standard hardware filters.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Measured Neutron Flux Profiles of the SAFARI-1 Research Reactor
comments: 33 pages, 26 figures, submitted to Annals of Nuclear Energy
summary: Knowledge of the neutron flux distribution is essential for safe and effective reactor utilisation. In the SAFARI-1 research reactor, a set of axial flux profiles are periodically measured by activating natural copper wires inserted along the height of the fuel or control assemblies and subsequently measuring their activity using a sodium iodide detector. Improper wire insertion can, however, result in profiles that do not accurately represent the actual neutron flux distribution. Building on previously identified potential indicators of improper wire insertion, an automated approach based on unsupervised learning was developed to detect anomalous axial flux measurements. The measured data were preprocessed using missing-value imputation, decay correction, and normalisation. High-order polynomial fitting was then applied to characterise the axial flux profiles and derive features describing their shape. The Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm was employed to group flux profiles into regular and abnormal clusters based on these features with results matching the known groups. In addition, Convolutional Autoencoders were developed and trained on flux profiles from central and peripheral core positions to identify deviations from the regular profiles through reconstruction error, achieving better performance in central assemblies than in peripheral assemblies. The developed framework is intended to provide feedback to reactor operation by identifying potential wire-insertion problems in the manual technique used for axial flux monitoring at SAFARI-1.
comment: 33 pages, 26 figures, submitted to Annals of Nuclear Energy

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
summary: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

title: Waveform-based pulse timing enhanced by self-supervised neural regression models for digital nuclear instrumentation
summary: With the rapid development of high-sampling-rate digital nuclear devices, their applications in nuclear facilities and related fields become more acceptable, and will possibly become widespread due to the versatility and flexibility of waveform sampling systems. When digitizers reach hundreds of megahertz or gigahertz, their lower limit in time measurement probes into the sub-nanosecond region, expediting their use in a bunch of time-critical scenarios. While conventional algorithms coupled with digital sampling techniques realize fair pulse timing in certain conditions, the potentials are still open to compact and efficient machine learning models. In this paper, we intend to boost the performance of pulse timing with a new paradigm of self-supervised learning on matched waveform pairs. The proposed method combines the mainstream self-supervised loss and the auxiliary weakly-supervised loss on the reference set, jointly improving the timing performance. We apply the method in a gamma/neutron-mixed radiation field, common in nuclear facilities. The simulation and experimental results show that, the proposed method not only outperforms conventional timing algorithms, but also surpasses neural network models based on supervised learning alone. Considering the trained model is lightweight and computationally efficient, it is promising to deploy it on edge devices, like economical microcontrollers with neural processing units.

title: Design and Experimental Evaluation of a Low-Cost Immersion Cooling System
comments: 20 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. CAD files: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SWZV7 ; firmware and data: https://github.com/koc003/Design-and-Experimental-Evaluation-of-a-Low-Cost-Immersion-Cooling-System-ESP32
summary: This paper presents a low-cost, open-source, single-phase immersion cooling testbed for studying liquid cooling of data center hardware. A 500 W titanium heater, standing in for server load, is submerged in a glass tank of mineral oil, a dielectric fluid. The heated oil is circulated by a magnetic drive pump through an air-cooled radiator. An ESP32 microcontroller logs three DS18B20 temperature sensors (heater surface, bulk fluid and ambient) and switches the pump, fan and heater through a relay module. The complete system costs INR 35,318 (about USD 380), built entirely from components available in India. At quasi-steady state under the full 500 W load, the heater surface reached 118.3 °C while the bulk oil stayed at 29.3 °C, only 8.0 °C above ambient. Thermal-resistance analysis shows that the heater-to-oil interface, limited by natural convection, accounts for about 92% of the total resistance (178.0 vs 16.0 m°C/W). The external loop therefore has spare capacity. CAD files, firmware and data are openly available, so the setup can be reproduced and used to compare dielectric fluids, loads and flow arrangements.
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. CAD files: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/SWZV7 ; firmware and data: https://github.com/koc003/Design-and-Experimental-Evaluation-of-a-Low-Cost-Immersion-Cooling-System-ESP32

title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
summary: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.

title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
summary: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $ρ= 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.

title: Methanol substitution suppresses deflagration-excited knock and increases the efficiency of a hydrogen-fuelled CFR engine
summary: Knock restricts the performance of hydrogen spark-ignition engines and is usually attributed to end-gas autoignition. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study in which methanol is used to replace part of the hydrogen in a hydrogen engine at constant fuel energy addition, and it shows that near the knock boundary the limiting oscillation is excited by the deflagration itself, which methanol removes without derating the performance. Port-injected methanol replaced 20--50% of the hydrogen energy in a variable-compression Cooperative Fuel Research engine at 600 rpm and compression ratios of 8--12. With pure hydrogen, oscillation in the 4--15 kHz range began before 10% of the charge had burned in 97--100% of cycles, and its maximum amplitude (MAPO) followed the maximum pressure-rise rate across 2499 cycles (Spearman $ρ=0.94$). Methanol slowed the deflagration: it replaced high-flame-speed hydrogen, cooled the intake by 24--25 K and, at unchanged intake pressure, enleaned the mixture by 10--13%. At 50% methanol, the 10--90% combustion duration lengthened 2.7--3.0-fold, oscillation onset moved 4.5--8.3$^\circ$CA after CA10 and mean MAPO fell by 89--93% although the spark timing was advanced by 13--19$^\circ$CA, and IMEP and indicated thermal efficiency rose by 2.4--7.8%. Methanol was thus worth more than this advance, and at matched CA50 MAPO was still about 90% lower. The measured combustion duration of all 25 data sets scaled with the computed laminar flame speed as $S_L^{-0.58}$ ($R^2=0.99$); fuel replacement accounted for about three quarters of the reduction in $S_L$, and the end-gas autoignition integral stayed below 0.07, against 1 at autoignition. The chamber kept its cylindrical acoustic modes, whose frequencies fell by 8--9%. The trade-off is formaldehyde emissions, which rose five- to sixfold while NO$_x$ fell by 49--85%.

title: Physical-Risk-Aware Decentralized Agents for Constrained Vehicle Communications
summary: Decentralized V2X resource control is challenging because each vehicle has only local observations, while reliability depends on network-wide interactions. We develop a physical-risk-aware spatio-temporal graph attention (PA-STGAT) framework for agentic V2X control. Each vehicle perceives its local interaction graph, retains short-term temporal context, and independently selects its PC5 resource and power. Network outcomes are used during centralized training to refine the shared policy. Transmitter-specific credits map reliability failures to individual vehicles. A dual-priced graph term further converts network violations into coordination signals for discrete resource selection, with higher priority on short time-to-collision links. Experiments show higher raw-policy reliability than the tested graph-based baselines. Under filtered execution, PA-STGAT meets the nominal empirical communication requirements across all five seeds, with tradeoffs among utility, delivery reliability, resource occupancy, and filter-induced repair. Compared with GNN+MATD3, it requires fewer resource repairs but achieves lower utility and mean delivery reliability. Mechanism ablations show that removing dual-priced graph coordination causes resource-selection collapse. Density and mobility tests characterize the operating limits of empirical constraint satisfaction.

title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
summary: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

title: Convergence Properties of PF-Exec: Homogeneous Structure, Anchored Closed Form, and Gain Dynamics
summary: This paper establishes a layered mathematical char acterisation of PF-Exec, the algorithm of the companion system paper. Demand-proportional bandwidth allocation yields an exact first-order homogeneous decomposition, from which the equal-load bandwidth target and its feasibility bound follow in closed form. The logarithmic knee view preserves strict load order and shares its global optimum with the Jain fairness index, while the demand-weighted centroid minimises the position potential. The damped softmax association block possesses a fixed point on the product of simplices. The truncated one-dimensional gain iteration admits a complete characterisation, with geomet ric convergence below the critical gain, initial-value-dependent bounded oscillation at it, and a family of bounded two-state cycles above it. A global invariant error ball and an explicit tracking recursion complete the execution guarantee. A numerical audit confirms the structural identities on every measured state and quantifies the local amplification of the coupled association and resource dynamics. Together, the results explain how closed form recovery directions and bounded adaptive gains provide stable execution without requiring a global Euclidean contraction assumption.

title: Isolation of $k$-cliques in uniform hypergraphs
summary: A copy of a hypergraph $F$ is called an $F$-copy. For any integers $k$ and $r$ with $2 \leq r \leq k$, let $K_k^r$ denote the complete $r$-uniform hypergraph whose vertex set is $[k] = \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ (that is, the edges of $K_k^r$ are the $r$-element subsets of $[k]$). Given an $r$-uniform $m$-edge hypergraph $H$, the $K_k^r$-isolation number of $H$, denoted by $ι(H, K_k^r)$, is the size of a smallest subset $D$ of the vertex set of $H$ such that the closed neighbourhood $N[D]$ of $D$ intersects the vertex sets of the $K_k^r$-copies contained by $H$ (equivalently, $H-N[D]$ contains no $K_k^r$-copy). We prove that if $H$ is connected and not a $K_k^r$-copy, then $$ι(H, K^r_k) \le \left \lfloor \frac{(r-1)m + 1}{(r-1)(\binom{k}{r}+1) + 1} \right \rfloor.$$ The bound is best possible. This is a solution to a problem of Li, Zhang and Ye. We also provide an alternative proof for $r < k$. Both proofs introduce new ideas for establishing bounds on isolation parameters.

title: A graph discretization of the Steklov and Neumann problems on domains in complete Riemannian manifolds
summary: We establish quantitative spectral convergence for graph discretizations of the Steklov and Neumann problems for bounded domains in complete Riemannian manifolds. Our construction uses weighted proximity graphs built from maximal $ε$-separated sets, with a correction to the discrete energy accounting for the geometry near the boundary. We consider two discrete Steklov problems: one defined using an averaged boundary trace, and the other using restriction to boundary vertices. Both approximate the continuum Steklov spectrum, but under different conditions on the discretization parameters. The additional scale condition required for the restriction-based problem is also necessary for spectral convergence. As a byproduct, we obtain quantitative convergence of the Neumann spectrum. The estimates are uniform under suitable geometric bounds.

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Dynamical Systems
comments: 19 pages, AIAA SciTech Forum 2027 (Uncertainty Quantification Conference)
summary: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.
comment: 19 pages, AIAA SciTech Forum 2027 (Uncertainty Quantification Conference)

title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for 2D XRD Interpretation Using Simulated and Experimental Data
summary: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with naïve fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.

title: Contrastive local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits
comments: 19 pages (13 main, 6 supplementary) and 11 figures (5 main, 6 supplementary)
summary: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges. The same local rule trains classifiers that reach the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit benchmarks, and a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. These results establish the feasibility of local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits.
comment: 19 pages (13 main, 6 supplementary) and 11 figures (5 main, 6 supplementary)

title: Finite speed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac processes and their applications in generative modeling
summary: We study the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac (OU-K) process, where instead of a Brownian motion, a finite-speed Kac process defines the driving process. The OU-K process can be analyzed through a rescaled, time-inhomogeneous Kac process, characterized by a switching rate from the Kac part, and a convergence rate from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) part. The law of this inhomogeneous Kac process describes the solution of a wave equation, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation. For Kac switching rates being multiples of the OU convergence rate, we can explicitly derive this EPD solution via the sum of (the derivative of) two Legendre polynomials, restricted between two Dirac points representing the wave fronts. Using the framework of piecewise-deterministic Markov processes (PDMP), we describe the conditional velocity fields of the OU-K process via our polynomial-law-formula. This allows us to apply the OU-K process in a generative flow model. Since the OU-K velocity fields prove to be bounded by the finite Kac speed, the usual time truncations of diffusion models become unnecessary. We demonstrate advantages over diffusion and flow matching models in terms of generation sharpness on singular data sets, while achieving competitive results on CIFAR-10 image generation.

title: A Unified Device-Level Physical Framework for DRAM Read Disturbance
summary: Read disturbance in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) depends on both local device interactions and the electrical conditions imposed by shared array circuitry. Here, we combine DIMM-level characterization results, device measurements, and TCAD simulations to interpret RowHammer, RowPress, and ColumnDisturb within a unified device-level physical framework. We relate charge evolution at the floating storage node to three key mechanisms: trap-assisted electron migration (EM), capacitive coupling (CC), and sense-amplifier-mediated disturb (SAMD). EM is local and trap-sensitive, while CC weakens with wordline separation. SAMD extends disturbance through shared column circuitry by modifying unselected-cell leakage under rail-level bitline biases, a contribution supported by the approximately ninefold higher OFF-state leakage measured relative to retention-like conditions for a high-voltage storage state. These distinct spatial ranges account for localized RowHammer and RowPress failures and remote ColumnDisturb populations with abrupt changes at subarray boundaries. We further interpret prolonged RowPress activation as a transition from an initial RowHammer-like transient to sustained leakage driven mainly by SAMD under held wordline and bitline biases. Within this device-level framework, trap effectiveness and storage-state-dependent leakage provide an interpretation of previously puzzling failure signatures, including the earlier onset of 0-to-1 RowHammer failures despite the predominance of 1-to-0 failures at high hammer counts. The same framework explains the observed RowPress and ColumnDisturb polarities and the duration-dependent reversal of neighboring- and passing-wordline effectiveness. These results provide a physical basis for developing compact DRAM reliability models across access patterns and array configurations.

title: Nonexistence of a quasi-symmetric $2$-$(33,15,35)$ design
summary: It is shown that there exists no quasi-symmetric $2$-$(33,15,35)$ design with intersection numbers $6$ and $9$. This is proved by considering the ternary code generated by the incidence vectors of the blocks and its dual code.

title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
comments: 27 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Submitted to International Transactions in Operational Research. Data, schedules, checkers and code: https://github.com/andrealbrechtl/agent-heuristics-jobshop-supplement/
summary: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Submitted to International Transactions in Operational Research. Data, schedules, checkers and code: https://github.com/andrealbrechtl/agent-heuristics-jobshop-supplement/

title: A Tumour-Aware Multimodal Framework for Explainable Prediction of IDH Mutation in Gliomas from Multi-Sequence MRI
comments: 45 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in International Journal of Information Technology & Decision Making (World Scientific)
summary: Accurate prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status is essential for glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. Although recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated promising performance, many rely on whole-brain feature extraction and provide limited interpretability. This study proposes a tumour-aware multimodal framework for explainable, non-invasive prediction of IDH mutation status from multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed framework integrates four MRI sequences (T1, T1CE, T2, and FLAIR), tumour subregion segmentation, quantitative radiomic descriptors, and clinical information within a unified deep learning architecture. An ablation study was conducted to evaluate the contribution of tumour-aware learning, radiomic features, and clinical variables. Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, balanced accuracy, receiver operating characteristic analysis, confusion matrix evaluation, and Grad-CAM visualisation. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed multimodal framework consistently outperformed the baseline MRI-only model, with the Clinical Fusion model achieving the strongest overall predictive performance. The integration of tumour-aware learning, radiomic descriptors, and clinical information progressively improved classification performance, while Grad-CAM visualisations indicated that the model predominantly focused on biologically relevant tumour regions. These findings suggest that tumour-aware multimodal feature integration enables accurate, interpretable, and non-invasive molecular profiling of gliomas and provides a promising foundation for future clinical decision support in precision neuro-oncology.
comment: 45 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables. Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in International Journal of Information Technology & Decision Making (World Scientific)

title: Proximal Adam algorithm for nonsmooth composite optimization and linear convergence under proximal PL geometry
summary: We analyze Adam-type methods for nonsmooth composite optimization problems $\min_xΦ(x)=f(x)+h(x)$, where $f$ is smooth and $h$ is convex, proper, and lower semicontinuous. The nonsmooth term is treated by a metric-weighted proximal map, while the smooth term is preconditioned by the Adam second-moment matrix. We prove a composite descent lemma whose constants depend explicitly on the spectral bounds of the adaptive metric and a residual--step equivalence that converts proximal step decay into subgradient stationarity. These yield an $O(1/N)$ bound on the minimum proximal stationarity residual for the deterministic proximal normalized gradient method without convexity of $f$, and the same $O(1/N)$ rate for proximal Adam under quantitative momentum-alignment and residual-coherence conditions together with a metric-compatibility condition. By estimating the momentum error directly, the same $O(1/N)$ rate is also obtained without the momentum-alignment and residual-coherence assumptions. When the composite objective satisfies a proximal Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequality, both algorithms and the relaxed proximal Adam scheme converge linearly with explicit contraction factors. Numerical experiments on a diagonal Lasso problem, two-dimensional image TV denoising, and two-dimensional elastic parameter identification illustrate the predicted stationarity and linear rates.

title: High-probability convergence of adaptive, proximal, and clipped Adam-type methods for nonconvex stochastic optimization
summary: This paper develops a unified high-probability analysis of adaptive, proximal, and clipped first-order methods for nonconvex stochastic optimization. For a smooth objective whose stochastic gradient error has sub-Gaussian norm, the normalized adaptive gradient method attains the standard stochastic nonconvex complexity of the square root of the number of iterations, with an additional logarithmic dependence on the inverse confidence level that is inversely proportional to the number of iterations. The proof uses an adaptive descent decomposition together with Freedman and Bernstein concentration inequalities. The same guarantee is established for the full adaptive moment method under an explicit momentum-alignment condition. The analysis is extended to projected and proximal updates through a stationarity measure based on the subdifferential distance, to objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, and to heavy-tailed noise through truncation. The framework is applied to stochastic inverse problems in elasticity, and numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical scaling and the practical behavior of the methods.

title: X-Strata: Separating Aneurysms and Overlapping Vessels into Layers from 2D X-ray Angiography
comments: 22 pages, including 10 pages of supplementary material
summary: An X-ray angiogram sums every structure along a ray into one pixel. When vessels cross an aneurysm, they obscure part of it and mix their contrast into its filling curve. We present X-Strata, a network that separates a cine angiogram into three layers: the complete aneurysm sac, the vessels in front of it, and the vessels behind it. Contrast timing indicates how much each layer contributes to a pixel, and parallax between two views indicates their order, which a single view cannot determine. X-Strata first estimates the layers and their contrast curves, then uses the second view to assign vessels to the front or back layer, and lifts all layers into 3D. It learns from layer labels projected from same-session 3D rotational angiography, but needs only 2D cine runs and their acquisition geometry at inference. On 220 held-out patients from three centers (122 external), two-view X-Strata ranks first among 14 baselines, including VGGT and C$^2$RV, in recovering the sac where vessels overlap it (Dice 0.693 internal, 0.641 external) and in ordering the layers (balanced accuracy 0.703, 0.659). Its order accuracy exceeds that of all 11 end-to-end baselines by at least 4.1 points internally and 3.3 externally (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$) and grows with view separation. Recovered 3D sac surfaces have a median Chamfer distance of 0.34 mm on the internal cohort. X-Strata may therefore provide layered aneurysm and vessel information, including 3D sac shape, for patients who undergo only 2D angiography.
comment: 22 pages, including 10 pages of supplementary material

title: The Polyak-Łojasiewicz Paper: A 10-Year Retrospective
summary: In 2016, we wrote a paper introducing the phrase "Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition" for an old idea, unsure of how readers would react. The paper ultimately had a larger impact than we expected, and we are surprised and honoured to receive the 2026 PKDD ECML Test of Time Award. With 10 years of hindsight, this note offers an informal and candid retrospective on the PL condition. We take a look back at the origins of the paper, give an AI-assisted refined version of the main theorem, review criticisms of the work, and discuss a variety of related ideas and extensions.

title: Tight Quantum Query Bounds for Collision Finding over Arbitrary Bounded Types
summary:
We determine the bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding one $r$-collision in an $N$-input function of prescribed type, which specifies all equality-class sizes. For every fixed maximum class size and collision order, we give a tight bound as the maximum of scales determined by the numbers of classes of size at least $2,\ldots,r$. The lower bound holds for a uniformly random function of that type, and a matching algorithm succeeds on every such function. No intermediate class size is required to occur, and every feasible output alphabet is allowed.
  The characterization connects the abundant-collision regime associated with set equality to the sparse-target regime of $k$-distinctness. In particular, finding the unique $(k+1)$-collision in type $(k^n,k+1)$ has complexity $Θ_k(N^{3/4-1/[4(2^{k+1}-1)]})$, where $N=kn+k+1$, resolving an open problem of Belovs.
  For the lower bound, we introduce a filtered compressed permutation oracle that projects onto a harmonic database subspace after each complete function query. Its $O(T/N)$ comparison error over $T$ queries overcomes the square-root limitation of the unfiltered process. Hidden capacity extensions and moment estimates retain the populations at each intermediate collision order. Matching upper bounds use sampled collision lists and colored adaptive learning graphs, with a coherent decision-to-search conversion that avoids logarithmic overhead. We also give an alternative nested quantum-walk algorithm for three-collision search, matching the bound up to polylogarithmic factors.

title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
summary: The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Niño, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Niño development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

title: HOL in HOL: mechanized soundness, completeness and consistency, with and without infinity
comments: 23 pages, 1 figure. Formal proof artifacts: Archive of Formal Proofs entries HOL_in_HOL_Deep and HOL_in_HOL_Deep_Infinity_ZFC (Isabelle2026). Submitted
summary: What can a logic certify about a copy of itself? For Church's simple theory of types, formalized as a deep embedding in Isabelle/HOL with Henkin semantics and a natural-deduction calculus, the answer has two tiers. On the first tier, plain Isabelle/HOL certifies the logic without an axiom of infinity, by a standard model with one individual. On the second tier, the logic with a Dedekind-style axiom of infinity is certified only in Isabelle/HOL extended by a large enough set-theoretic universe. Both tiers appear in Harrison's self-verification of HOL Light. What the present formalization adds is Henkin completeness, and with it a semantics that matches the calculus exactly, compactness and model existence on the first tier, and the boundary between the tiers. Comparing two ways of adding infinity to the object logic shows where the boundary lies. One is an infinite domain of individuals, expressed by the first-order sentences "there are at least $n$ individuals", each of which has a finite model; the other is the Dedekind axiom, a single sentence with no finite model, and there the first tier ends. In the calculus the axiom is strictly stronger than the sentences together: it derives each of them, but they do not derive it. The witness is a countable Henkin model in which every sentence holds and the axiom fails, because its function domain is too sparse for an injective, non-surjective self-map. On the second tier, the universe serves one purpose only: to prove the Dedekind axiom consistent. Everything that follows, completeness and even the countable Henkin model of the axiom, is obtained in plain Isabelle/HOL. The universe axiom is Harrison-style, realized in Paulson's ZFC_in_HOL with the domain of every type in $V_{ω+ω}$; with it, full classical higher-order logic with infinity and relational choice is consistent relative to set theory.
comment: 23 pages, 1 figure. Formal proof artifacts: Archive of Formal Proofs entries HOL_in_HOL_Deep and HOL_in_HOL_Deep_Infinity_ZFC (Isabelle2026). Submitted

title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
summary: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph.
